title: Twenty-five years
hookLine: Ananda's decades as attendant, bringing water, keeping the door
carry: like a shadow that never leaves

cards: Some jobs leave no record but the person doing them. The cup is filled, the door is answered, the visitor waits the right amount of time, and none of it gets written down. Ananda's job was that kind.
In the verses the Theragatha gives him, he does something unexpected. He counts. Not his insights, not his sermons: his years of service.
Twenty-five of them, he says, at the Buddha's side. And he says what kind of years they were.

teach.h: LIKE A SHADOW THAT NEVER LEAVES.
teach.b: First, the shadow. In paraphrase, Ananda says: for twenty-five years I attended the Blessed One with loving deeds, like a shadow that never leaves. Then he says it again for loving speech, and again for loving thoughts.
Body, words, mind: service all the way through.
Second, the water. In the long discourse on the Buddha's last journey, the old teacher is tired and thirsty by a little stream and asks Ananda for a drink. Ananda hesitates.
Carts have just crossed, he says, and churned it up. There's a clear river not far on. The Buddha asks again, and again.
So Ananda goes, bowl in hand, and finds the stream running clear. Even a devoted attendant sometimes has to be asked three times, and goes. Third, the night watch.
In the Udana, the monks are gathered for their observance night. The Buddha sits in silence, and the night wears on.
Late in the night Ananda gets up, arranges his robe, and says, in paraphrase: Lord, the night is far gone, the monks have been sitting a long time. Will you recite the rule for them?
He's keeping time for everyone in the room.
Fourth, the perks he turned down.
The commentaries tell that when Ananda agreed to be attendant, he asked for conditions.
Tradition says he asked not to be given the Buddha's robes or food, or a place in his lodging, so no one could say he served for the benefits.
He asked instead to bring visitors to the Buddha, and to hear any teaching he'd missed. The service, by that story, was the whole point.

how: In Buddhist monasteries, junior monks and nuns may attend their teachers, bringing water and food and caring for their needs, and Ananda is remembered as the model attendant.

o: how long Ananda trained before ordination
the length of the Buddha's whole teaching life
how long Ananda says he attended the Buddha

games.q: Ananda the attendant: tap the pairs.

s: Ananda fetched the water the first time he was asked
he said carts had churned the stream and suggested a river further on. asked again, he went and found it clear.
in his verses Ananda compares himself to a shadow that never leaves
for twenty-five years, in deed, word and thought.
tradition says Ananda took the post for the Buddha's robes and food
the commentaries say he asked not to be given them.

games.q: you're Ananda. your old teacher is thirsty and asks for water, but carts have just churned up the nearby stream. what do you say?
o: say there's a clear river not far on.
tell him to wait until morning.
games.why: he suggests the river. the Buddha asks again, and again. Ananda goes to the stream and finds it running clear.

practice: Think of one person you'll be around today and a small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: refill the water, clear the sink, hold a door.
Hold it in mind the way Ananda served, with hands, words and a kind thought, and let the wish to be thanked come up and go by.

wordCard.voice: Twenty-five years. In his own verses, Ananda counts the years he attended the Buddha, in deed, word and thought, like a shadow that never leaves. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: attendant, one who stands near to serve; the role Ananda held.

carryVoice: Your line: like a shadow that never leaves. In deed, in word, in thought. Day seven hundred thirty-three, done.
